step: Employer files partial residence permit application via Enter Finland (TTOL)
deadline_label: At least 90 days before target start date
non_obvious_official_guidance: The employer must submit the employer's partial application through Enter Finland before the employee can begin their part of the residence permit application.
non_obvious_actual_reality: HR generalists routinely try to start with the employee's application and find the system blocks it until Migri has received the employer's part. Missing this step by even a week can push the start date by a month or more.
non_obvious_action_required: Create or log in to an employer account at enterfinland.fi, complete and submit the employer's partial application, and share the resulting application reference number with the employee so they can link their submission.
source: Migri – Residence permit for an employed person

step: Third-country national applies for residence permit for an employed person (oleskelulupa)
form_name: OLE_TY1 – Employee's part of residence permit application
deadline_label: After employer partial application is submitted; allow 90 days standard processing
source: Migri – Residence permit for an employed person

step: Employer applies for A1 certificate to keep EU/EEA posted employee in home-country social security
authority: Home-country social security institution (e.g. home-country Kela equivalent)
field_label: Social security — A1 certificate of coverage
deadline_label: Before the employee's departure — ideally 30 days in advance
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under EU Regulation 883/2004, a worker posted to another EU/EEA country for up to 24 months may remain in their home-country social security system if the employer obtains an A1 certificate from the competent home-country institution before the employee departs.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Without an A1 certificate the employee falls into Finnish social security from day one and the employer owes Finnish social contributions simultaneously with any home-country commitments. Retroactive A1 applications are administratively complex and may not be accepted by Kela.
non_obvious_action_required: Before the employee's last working day at home, the employer applies to the home-country social security authority for an A1. The certificate must exist and be presented before departure. If granted, share a copy with the employee and retain it — Kela and the employer's Finnish payroll team will both need to see it.
source: Kela – Social security when working in another EU/EEA country

step: Employee obtains European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) from home country before departure
deadline_label: Before departure — allow up to 14 days for card delivery

step: Foreign employer submits posted worker notification to AVI before work begins in Finland
deadline_label: Before or on the day the employee first works in Finland
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under the Finnish Posted Workers Act (laki lähetetyistä työntekijöistä, 447/2016), a foreign employer sending workers to Finland must file a notification with AVI before work commences.
non_obvious_actual_reality: HR generalists frequently confuse a posted worker (employee of a foreign employer on a temporary assignment) with a locally hired employee. The notification obligation applies only to genuine postings. Filing it unnecessarily or missing it entirely when it is required both create compliance risk — fines apply for late or absent notification.
non_obvious_action_required: Determine the legal structure: if the employer is a foreign entity and the employee is temporarily assigned to Finland (not hired locally by a Finnish entity), file the notification via the AVI portal at ilmoitusvelvollisuus.fi before the employee's first working day. Retain confirmation.
source: AVI – Posted Workers Act notification obligation

step: EU/EEA national registers right of residence at Migri
form_name: OLE_REK – Registration of right of residence
field_label: EU/EEA residency — right of residence registration
deadline_label: Within 3 months of arrival in Finland
non_obvious_official_guidance: EU/EEA nationals exercising free movement rights in Finland must register their right of residence at Migri if they intend to stay for more than three months.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Many EU nationals assume free movement means zero registration formalities. In practice, the right of residence certificate issued by Migri is a prerequisite for DVV to register the person in the population information system and issue a henkilötunnus — skipping Migri blocks every downstream step including the tax card and Kela enrolment.
non_obvious_action_required: Apply via enterfinland.fi and book an in-person appointment at the nearest Migri service point as soon as possible after arrival — before the 3-month deadline. Bring a valid passport or national ID, employment contract or employer certificate, and proof of accommodation.
source: Migri – EU citizen registration of right of residence

step: Book DVV appointment immediately on arrival to obtain Finnish personal identity code (henkilötunnus)
authority: Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV / Digi- ja väestötietovirasto)
deadline_label: Book on arrival day — wait times are 2–4 weeks in major cities
non_obvious_official_guidance: The henkilötunnus is issued after an in-person visit to a DVV service point where identity documents are verified; the process cannot be completed entirely online.
non_obvious_actual_reality: DVV appointments in Helsinki and other major cities are frequently fully booked 2–4 weeks ahead. Employees who wait until they feel settled often find their first payslip arrives before the henkilötunnus is issued, which means the tax card cannot be obtained in time and the employer must apply the 60% emergency withholding rate.
non_obvious_action_required: Go to dvv.fi/en and book the earliest available in-person appointment on arrival day or within the first 24 hours in Finland. Gather required documents in advance: passport, Finnish residence permit sticker or Migri right of residence certificate, proof of address (rental contract), and employment contract.
source: DVV – Registering in the Finnish Population Information System

step: Attend DVV appointment and receive Finnish personal identity code (henkilötunnus)
authority: Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV)
deadline_label: At DVV appointment (typically 2–4 weeks after arrival)

step: Register domicile (kotikunta) in the Finnish Population Register at the DVV appointment
authority: Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV)
deadline_label: At DVV appointment — same visit as henkilötunnus
source: DVV – Registering in the Finnish Population Information System

step: Apply for Finnish tax card (verokortti) from Vero before first payslip is processed
deadline_label: Before the employer processes the employee's first payslip
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employees must obtain a tax card from Vero and provide it to their employer; without a valid tax card the employer is legally required to withhold tax at the emergency rate.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Finland's emergency (toimitusprosentti) withholding rate is 60%. An employee who misses this step will lose a significant portion of their first salary or more. Reclaiming overpaid tax requires filing the annual return and waiting for the Vero assessment — typically the following year.
non_obvious_action_required: Apply via OmaVero at vero.fi as soon as the henkilötunnus is issued. Enter estimated annual income and the employer's Finnish Business ID (Y-tunnus) so Vero can transmit the card electronically to payroll. Do not wait for the employer to request it — the obligation is the employee's.
source: Vero – Tax card for foreign employees coming to Finland

step: Register for Finnish tax number (veronumero) — mandatory for all workers on Finnish construction or shipyard sites
field_label: Construction compliance — tax number and photo ID
deadline_label: Before the employee's first day on a Finnish construction or shipyard site
non_obvious_official_guidance: All workers present on Finnish construction and shipyard sites must carry and display a photo ID bearing their Finnish tax number. Employers must report every worker on their sites to Vero via the employer reporting system.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The obligation applies to every worker on site regardless of nationality, employer country, or visit duration — including subcontractors and posted workers present for a single day. A worker without a displayed tax number ID can be removed from the site immediately and the employer faces fines. Many HR generalists are unaware this is separate from the ordinary tax card.
non_obvious_action_required: Apply for the tax number through OmaVero at vero.fi immediately after the henkilötunnus is issued. Once registered, the tax number must be incorporated into the worker's site photo ID card. This requirement applies only to construction and shipyard worksites — not office-based roles.

step: Register with Kela for Finnish social security coverage — only if no valid A1 certificate is held
authority: Social Insurance Institution of Finland (Kela / Kansaneläkelaitos)
non_obvious_official_guidance: Employees working in Finland are generally subject to Finnish social security legislation from the start of employment and should register with Kela.
non_obvious_actual_reality: EU/EEA employees holding a valid A1 certificate from their home country remain in their home-country social security for the posted period and must NOT register with Kela — doing so would create a double-contribution conflict. Third-country nationals and EU/EEA employees without an A1 must register with Kela, and the employer owes Finnish social insurance contributions.
non_obvious_action_required: Before arrival, confirm whether the employee holds an A1 certificate. If yes, no Kela registration is needed for the duration covered by the A1. If no A1, register with Kela using form Y 38e (EU/EEA) or Y 77e (non-EU) at a Kela office or by post, presenting the DVV registration confirmation, passport, and employment contract.
source: Kela – Moving to Finland for work

step: Register with local health centre (terveysasema) for Finnish public healthcare
authority: Municipal health centre (terveysasema) / Wellbeing Services County (hyvinvointialue)
form_name: No national form — contact local health centre directly
deadline_label: After DVV domicile registration is processed
non_obvious_official_guidance: Persons registered in the Finnish population register by DVV and resident in Finland are entitled to use municipal health services in their registered municipality of domicile.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Entitlement to public healthcare is not automatic upon arrival — it activates only once the DVV domicile registration is confirmed and processed. Employees who need healthcare before that point should use their home-country EHIC or private travel insurance. The assigned health centre is determined by the registered residential address, not by employer location.
non_obvious_action_required: After receiving DVV confirmation that domicile registration is complete, identify the health centre assigned to the registered home address via the local municipality or wellbeing services county website. Contact that centre to register as a new patient.
source: DVV – Registering in the Finnish Population Information System

step: Monitor 183-day presence threshold — employee becomes Finnish tax resident subject to progressive taxation
form_name: Updated progressive tax card via OmaVero
deadline_label: Day 183 of Finnish presence in any rolling 12-month period
non_obvious_official_guidance: Under Finnish income tax law, a non-resident who stays in Finland for more than 183 days within a 12-month period is treated as tax resident and is subject to progressive income tax on Finland-sourced income.
non_obvious_actual_reality: The 183-day count runs over any rolling 12-month period, not the Finnish calendar year. An employee who arrives in October and remains through the following April can cross the threshold mid-fiscal-year while payroll is still set up for the flat 35% non-resident rate — creating an under-withholding liability that surfaces at tax assessment.
non_obvious_action_required: Track Finnish presence days from day one. When the employee approaches day 183, instruct them to apply for an updated progressive-rate tax card via OmaVero, and alert the payroll team to switch from the non-resident flat rate to the progressive withholding table immediately.
source: Vero – Taxation of employees from abroad

step: Employer assesses permanent establishment (PE) risk arising from employee activity in Finland
form_name: No specific form — employer corporate tax assessment
deadline_label: Before employee commences work; review again at 6-month mark
non_obvious_official_guidance: A foreign company whose employee regularly exercises authority to conclude contracts on its behalf in Finland, or whose employee constitutes a fixed place of business, may create a permanent establishment taxable in Finland under the applicable bilateral tax treaty.
non_obvious_actual_reality: PE risk rarely surfaces during routine relocation planning — it sits with legal and tax counsel, who are frequently not looped into HR-managed relocations. A single employee working from home in Finland in a client-facing or contract-authority role for a sustained period can inadvertently expose the foreign employer to Finnish corporate tax obligations.
non_obvious_action_required: Before the employee's start date, have the company's international tax advisor review the role description against the Finland tax treaty with the employer's home country. Document the assessment. Revisit the analysis at the 6-month mark or if the employee's responsibilities change materially.

step: File Finnish annual tax return (veroilmoitus / esitäytetty veroilmoitus)
form_name: Pre-completed tax return (esitäytetty veroilmoitus) via OmaVero
field_label: Tax compliance — annual income tax return
deadline_label: Typically May of the following calendar year (individual deadline stated on Vero pre-completed return)

step: Third-country national applies for continued residence permit (jatkolupa) before expiry
deadline_label: At least 3 months before the current permit expires

step: EU/EEA national applies for permanent right of residence after 5 continuous years in Finland
form_name: OLE_PY – Permanent right of residence registration
field_label: Long-term residency — permanent right of residence
deadline_label: Eligible after 5 years of continuous lawful residence — application is voluntary but advisable
non_obvious_official_guidance: EU/EEA nationals who have legally resided in Finland for five continuous years are entitled to apply for a permanent right of residence, which is not subject to the conditions attached to the temporary right of residence.
non_obvious_actual_reality: Many EU nationals who have been in Finland for years are unaware this status exists or that obtaining it removes the need for ongoing registration renewals and provides residency security independent of employment status — highly relevant if the employee's role changes or a gap in employment occurs.
non_obvious_action_required: After five years of continuous lawful residence, apply in person at a Migri service point with documentation of the five-year period (e.g. DVV population register extract, employment records, tax assessments). The application is voluntary but provides significant long-term administrative simplicity.
source: Migri – Permanent right of residence for EU citizens
